exercises.title: Build Tool Vocabulary - Webpack, Vite & Bundlers
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for Webpack, Vite, Rollup, and esbuild: bundles, chunks, tree shaking, and source maps.

questions.q: Tree shaking in a JavaScript bundler means:
options: Removing all console.log statements from production builds.
Eliminating dead code - unused exported functions, classes, and variables are not included in the final bundle, reducing its size.
Splitting the application code into separate files for each route.
Minifying the bundle by replacing long variable names with shorter ones.
questions.explanation: Tree shaking (a form of dead code elimination) relies on ES module static analysis. If you import { format } from 'date-fns', only the format function is bundled - not the entire date-fns library. Requires ES modules (not CommonJS).

questions.q: Code splitting in Webpack or Vite refers to:
options: Splitting the source code into separate Git repositories.
Breaking the application bundle into smaller chunks that can be loaded on demand - reducing initial page load size by deferring code for routes or features not immediately needed.
Separating test code from production code in the build output.
Splitting a large component file into multiple smaller files.
questions.explanation: Code splitting: instead of one large bundle, the app loads a small initial bundle and lazy-loads additional chunks when routes or features are accessed. Example: the admin dashboard chunk is only downloaded when the user navigates to /admin.

questions.q: Vite's key advantage over Webpack in development mode is:
options: Vite supports more programming languages than Webpack.
Vite serves source files as native ES modules during development - no bundling required, so the dev server starts instantly and HMR (hot module replacement) updates only the changed module.
Vite produces smaller production bundles than Webpack.
Vite does not require any configuration to use TypeScript.
questions.explanation: Vite's dev server exploits native browser ES modules: it serves untransformed modules and only transforms what the browser requests. No full bundle rebuild needed - HMR is fast because only the changed module is re-executed, not the whole app.

questions.q: A source map file in a JavaScript build is used to:
options: Map the structure of the source code directory for documentation purposes.
Map minified/transpiled production code back to the original source code - enabling browser DevTools to show the original file names, line numbers, and variable names when debugging.
Track which source files changed between builds for incremental compilation.
Map npm package names to their installed file locations.
questions.explanation: Source maps (.map files) allow debugging minified production code: the browser loads both the minified bundle and its source map, then shows original TypeScript/JSX in DevTools. External source maps (not inline) can be deployed separately for security - they reveal source code to anyone who accesses them.

questions.q: The phrase 'the production build was 2.3MB before tree shaking; after enabling tree shaking it dropped to 890KB' means:
options: The build tool compressed the files after tree shaking, reducing file size.
Unused exports from imported modules were eliminated, meaning 1.4MB of dead code was being bundled unnecessarily - tree shaking removed code that was never called.
The minifier replaced variable names with shorter ones, reducing the bundle size.
The application was split into multiple chunks that together total 890KB.
questions.explanation: A 61% size reduction from tree shaking indicates significant unused code in dependencies. This is common with large utility libraries (lodash, moment.js) - importing a single function but bundling the entire library. Tree shaking plus selective imports (import { format } not import everything) prevents this.

questions.q: The difference between Rollup and Webpack is best described as:
options: Rollup is for CSS bundling; Webpack is for JavaScript bundling.
Rollup is designed for bundling JavaScript libraries with clean ES module output; Webpack is designed for bundling complex web applications with many assets, loaders, and plugins.
Rollup is a newer tool that has entirely replaced Webpack in modern projects.
Webpack can only bundle CommonJS modules; Rollup only bundles ES modules.
questions.explanation: Rollup produces clean, flat ES module output - preferred for library authors (Vue, React, and many npm packages are built with Rollup). Webpack has richer plugin ecosystems for complex app bundling (CSS modules, asset handling, dev server). Vite uses Rollup for production builds.

exercises.title: Docker Compose Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn to read and write Docker Compose configuration in English: services, volumes, networks, and environment variable language.

questions.q: In Docker Compose, a 'service' definition describes:
options: A microservice deployed to a Kubernetes cluster.
A container configuration including its image, ports, environment variables, and dependencies.
An API endpoint exposed by the application.
A background worker process in a message queue.
questions.explanation: A service in docker-compose.yml defines everything needed to run one container: image, build context, ports, volumes, environment, and depends_on.

questions.q: The 'depends_on' key in a service definition means:
options: The service requires a paid Docker subscription.
This service will not start until the listed services have started.
This service uses a shared volume from another service.
The service depends on an external API being available.
questions.explanation: 'depends_on' controls startup order - a web service with 'depends_on: [db]' will wait for the db service to start before it launches.

questions.q: A Docker Compose 'named volume' is used to:
options: Give a container a memorable name for easy access.
Persist data outside the container lifecycle so data survives container restarts and recreation.
Share environment variables between services.
Tag a specific version of a Docker image.
questions.explanation: Named volumes (e.g., db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data) persist container data on the host - without volumes, data is lost when the container is removed.

questions.q: What does 'ports: - 5432:5432' in a service definition mean?
options: The service requires 5432 MB of memory.
Map host port 5432 to container port 5432, making the service accessible at localhost:5432.
The service runs 5432 container instances.
The container will start 5432 seconds after the host starts.
questions.explanation: Port mapping format is HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT. 5432:5432 exposes the container's port 5432 on the host's port 5432 - standard for PostgreSQL.

questions.q: The command 'docker compose up -d' means:
options: Stop and remove all containers defined in compose.
Start all services defined in docker-compose.yml in detached mode (background).
Build Docker images without starting containers.
Display logs for all running services.
questions.explanation: 'docker compose up' starts all services. The '-d' (detached) flag runs them in the background, returning control to the terminal.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I've added a new service, 'message_queue', to our Compose file. It needs to connect to the 'database' service, but it shouldn't start until the database is running. I'm using depends_on ."
options: The `depends_on` key tells Docker Compose that `message_queue` should be restarted whenever the `database` service stops.
The `depends_on` key instructs Docker Compose to automatically create a network interface for `message_queue` before it starts, improving performance.
The `depends_on` key specifies that `message_queue` will attempt to connect to the `database` service immediately upon starting, regardless of its current state.
The `depends_on` key indicates that `message_queue` should wait for the `database` service to reach a certain health status before proceeding with its own initialization.
questions.explanation: This is a common use case. The depends_on keyword in Docker Compose defines dependencies between services. It ensures that the `message_queue` service will only start *after* the `database` service has successfully started and is considered healthy. Importantly, it doesn't force immediate connection attempts; instead, it manages the startup order based on these defined relationships. Misconceptions often arise from thinking it's a restart mechanism - it's about sequential dependency resolution.

questions.q: John : 'I'm reviewing this PR. The `web_app` service is defined with `environment:` variables like `DATABASE_URL`. It seems a bit odd to hardcode the URL directly in the Compose file - shouldn't we use an external configuration source, maybe a secrets manager or environment variable passed during deployment?', Maria : 'We're using Docker Compose for development and it simplifies things. We can just put the database connection string in the `environment` block.'
options: insufficient - Maria is prioritizing ease of setup over best practices.
correct - hardcoding sensitive information like database URLs directly into the Compose file is a major security vulnerability that should be avoided.

partially correct - while using an external configuration source is generally recommended for production, it's acceptable in Docker Compose for development due to its simplicity and reduced operational overhead.
incorrect - Maria's approach is perfectly secure as long as the database server itself is properly secured.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a common debate about security versus developer convenience. While hardcoding configuration in Docker Compose is often acceptable for development to simplify local testing, it's generally considered a poor practice for production environments due to potential exposure of sensitive data like database credentials. Using external sources like secrets managers or environment variables passed during deployment provides better control, auditing capabilities, and reduces the risk of accidental leakage.

questions.q: David : 'Okay team, I've updated the `docker-compose.yml` file for our new microservice, 'payment_processor'. I've added a `restart: always` directive to the service definition. This should ensure it automatically restarts if it crashes, right? I'm not sure what that does exactly .
options: restart: always ensures the container only starts when there are no other running containers of the same name.
restart: always instructs Docker Compose to restart the container regardless of its exit code or resource constraints.
restart: always prevents the container from restarting automatically, even if it crashes.
restart: always is equivalent to setting `healthcheck` to 'false'.
questions.explanation: The `restart: always` directive in Docker Compose tells Docker to automatically restart the service container if it exits for any reason. This is crucial for ensuring high availability and resilience; it addresses a common pitfall where services might stop unexpectedly due to crashes or unexpected terminations. It's important to differentiate this from other restart policies like `on-failure` which only restarts on failure, and `no` which prevents restarting entirely.

questions.q: Context: The team is discussing a recent change to the `api_gateway` service's configuration within their Docker Compose setup. They've updated the `docker-compose.yml` file to include `depends_on` for the `database` service. PR Description: Subject: Update `api_gateway` service to use a new database connection. Body: > I've updated the `docker-compose.yml` file for the `api_gateway` service. The previous configuration used a hardcoded environment variable for the database URL, but I've now added a `depends_on` directive to ensure it starts after the `database` service is ready.
options: Adding depends_on automatically configures the database URL using a default value, ensuring the API gateway always has access to the database regardless of its initial state.

Using depends_on guarantees that the `api_gateway` service will attempt to connect to the database immediately upon startup, even if the database isn't fully initialized, potentially leading to connection errors.

Adding depends_on tells Docker Compose to create a new volume named 'database-data' automatically for storing the `api_gateway` service's database files, improving performance by avoiding disk I/O on the host machine.

Using depends_on ensures that the `api_gateway` service will only start *after* the `database` service has successfully started and is ready to accept connections, preventing potential errors during initialization.
questions.explanation: The correct answer (3) accurately describes the function of `depends_on`. It forces the `api_gateway` service to wait for the `database` service to reach a running state before attempting to start itself. The other options misinterpret the purpose: defaults are not automatically configured by `depends_on`, immediate connection attempts can cause errors, and `depends_on` does *not* create volumes - it controls startup order.

exercises.title: GitHub Actions Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn GitHub Actions vocabulary: workflows, jobs, steps, runners, secrets, and trigger event language.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, a 'workflow' is:
options: A single command executed on the runner.
A YAML-defined automated process triggered by events, containing one or more jobs.
A GitHub repository branch protection rule.
A manual deployment script run by the team.
questions.explanation: A workflow is the top-level GitHub Actions concept - a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that defines triggers, jobs, and steps for automated CI/CD processes.

questions.q: The 'runs-on' key in a GitHub Actions job specifies:
options: The Docker image used for the job.
The type of runner (virtual machine) the job executes on, such as ubuntu-latest or windows-latest.
The GitHub user account running the workflow.
The branch the job is triggered from.
questions.explanation: 'runs-on' defines the runner environment - GitHub provides hosted runners (ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest) or you can use self-hosted runners.

questions.q: A GitHub Actions 'secret' is:
options: A private GitHub repository.
An encrypted environment variable stored securely in GitHub and accessible to workflows without exposing the value in logs.
A workflow that runs only for internal team members.
A step that is hidden from the workflow run log.
questions.explanation: Secrets store sensitive values (API keys, credentials) securely. They are masked in logs and accessible to workflows via the secrets context: ${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}

questions.q: The 'on: push: branches: [main]' trigger in a workflow means:
options: The workflow runs when any branch is deleted.
The workflow is triggered every time code is pushed to the main branch.
The workflow only runs for pull requests to main.
The workflow runs manually from the Actions tab.
questions.explanation: The 'on' key defines triggers. 'push: branches: [main]' fires the workflow on every push directly to the main branch.

questions.q: What does 'needs' do in a GitHub Actions workflow with multiple jobs?
options: Specifies the required Node.js version for the job.
Creates a dependency between jobs so the dependent job waits for the listed jobs to succeed before starting.
Lists the GitHub Actions Marketplace actions used in the job.
Specifies the minimum GitHub plan required to run the workflow.
questions.explanation: 'needs' creates job dependencies - a 'deploy' job with 'needs: build' will only run after the 'build' job completes successfully.

questions.q: Mark suggests adding an `always` trigger to Sarah's GitHub Actions workflow. Sarah is concerned about the workflow's execution time and wants to minimize unnecessary runs. She's questioning whether a general `runs-on` directive targeting 'ubuntu-latest' will adequately handle both successful and failed job outcomes, or if more granular control within the workflow itself is required. Specifically, she wonders if the default Ubuntu environment provides sufficient logging capabilities for all potential scenarios without requiring explicit conditional logic.
options: The `always` trigger automatically scales resources based on the outcome, optimizing execution time regardless of success or failure.
Using a general `runs-on` directive ensures consistent logging across all environments, eliminating the need for specific conditions within the workflow.
Sarah's concern is misplaced; the `always` trigger simply guarantees that *some* logging will occur, regardless of the job's outcome, which is always beneficial.

The `runs-on` directive targeting 'ubuntu-latest' provides sufficient logging capabilities for handling both success and failure scenarios, and explicitly defining conditions within the workflow would add unnecessary complexity.
questions.explanation: Sarah's question highlights a key distinction: the `always` trigger guarantees *some* logging execution regardless of the job's status, while a general `runs-on` directive relies on the default Ubuntu environment for logging. While Ubuntu provides basic logging, it might not be sufficient for complex failure scenarios requiring specific diagnostics or detailed error reporting. Explicit conditions within the workflow offer more targeted control over logging based on the actual outcome.

questions.q: Liam in the code review says: 'This action is running on a small VM. Can we specify runs-on: ubuntu-latest to improve build speed?' What does Liam likely mean by ' ubuntu-latest '?
options: A. A specific version of Ubuntu, ensuring consistent builds.
B. The most recent Ubuntu distribution, providing the latest packages and updates.
C. A virtual machine with a dedicated IP address for testing.
D. A pre-configured environment optimized for JavaScript development.
questions.explanation: runs-on: ubuntu-latest refers to using the newest stable version of Ubuntu as the execution environment for the GitHub Action. This ensures that the action benefits from the most up-to-date packages and security patches, contributing to faster build times and more reliable results. Option A is incorrect because 'ubuntu-latest' doesn't specify a *version*.

questions.q: During a Slack conversation about debugging a failing GitHub Action, David asks: 'How do I check the logs generated by an action during its execution?' Which of the following options correctly describes how to view these logs?
options: A. Using the git log command within the repository.
B. Examining the runs-on configuration file for error messages.
C. Navigating to the GitHub Actions dashboard and selecting 'Logs' for the specific workflow run.
D. Running a grep command against the entire codebase.
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions provides a dedicated 'Logs' section within the workflow run on the GitHub Actions dashboard. This is the standard and most effective way to view detailed logs generated during an action's execution - this is what David needs. git log and grep are not designed for this purpose, and checking the runs-on file won't show runtime logs.

questions.q: In a PR description for a new GitHub Action that automatically deploys code to staging, Chloe writes: 'This action is triggered on every push to the develop branch and uses the deploy_staging secret.' What role does the deploy_staging secret likely play?
options: A. It identifies the specific Git repository being deployed.
B. It provides credentials for accessing the staging environment's deployment server.
C. It defines the name of the branch that triggers the action.
D. It specifies the version of the deployment tool to use.
questions.explanation: The deploy_staging secret is almost certainly a credential (e.g., an API key or password) used to authenticate with the staging environment's deployment server. This allows the action to securely deploy code without hardcoding sensitive information directly in the workflow definition. Option A is incorrect; the trigger defines the branch.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, Ethan says: 'I'm using a GitHub Action that runs every time someone opens an issue in the bugtracker project.' What does Ethan likely mean by 'runs every time someone opens an issue'?
options: A. The action automatically creates a new branch for each issue.
B. The action triggers a workflow based on a webhook event when a new issue is created.
C. The action sends a notification to the project team whenever an issue is opened.
D. The action automatically assigns a developer to each newly opened issue.
questions.explanation: Ethan describes a GitHub Action triggered by a 'webhook event'. When someone creates a new issue in the bugtracker project (through the GitHub API), this triggers a webhook that calls the action. This is the standard way to automate responses to events within GitHub - Option B is correct.

questions.q: Fiona asks you about using 'needs' in a multi-job GitHub Actions workflow. She wants to ensure that Job A completes successfully before Job B starts. Which of the following best describes the purpose of the 'needs' keyword?
options: A. It defines the order in which jobs execute sequentially.
B. It allows one job to depend on the completion of another job, ensuring dependencies are met.
C. It sets a time limit for how long a job can run before it's automatically canceled.
D. It specifies the environment variables that each job should use.
questions.explanation: 'Needs' establishes a dependency between GitHub Actions jobs. This means Job B will not start until Job A has successfully completed its execution - ensuring proper workflow orchestration and preventing potential errors caused by incomplete dependencies. Option D is incorrect; 'needs' defines *dependencies*, not environment variables.

exercises.title: Linter & Formatter Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn ESLint, Prettier, and linting vocabulary: rules, configs, auto-fix, and integrating linting into your workflow.

questions.q: An ESLint 'rule' set to 'error' will:
options: Suggest a fix but allow the build to proceed.
Cause ESLint to report a linting error and fail the CI check.
Automatically fix the issue without any output.
Add a warning to the console but not affect the build.
questions.explanation: ESLint severity levels: 'off' (disabled), 'warn' (warning, non-blocking), 'error' (error, blocks CI). Rules set to 'error' fail the lint check.

questions.q: Prettier is primarily a:
options: Security scanner for JavaScript code.
Opinionated code formatter that enforces consistent style by reformatting code automatically.
Linter that finds logical errors in code.
Type checker for TypeScript projects.
questions.explanation: Prettier formats code automatically - it does not check logic but enforces consistent style (indentation, quotes, line length) across the codebase.

questions.q: What does 'eslint --fix' do?
options: Removes all ESLint rules from the configuration.
Automatically fixes auto-fixable rule violations in the source files.
Generates a new ESLint configuration file.
Disables ESLint for the current project.

questions.q: What does 'devcontainer ensures everyone has the same environment' mean?
options: Everyone must use the same OS
A Dev Container configuration defines a reproducible Docker-based development environment so all developers have identical tools and settings
The container replaces version control
All developers share a single remote server
questions.explanation: Dev Containers (defined by .devcontainer/ config) use Docker to provide a consistent development environment with the same tools, extensions, and settings for all team members, eliminating 'works on my machine' issues.

questions.q: A developer says 'the dotenv file configures local secrets'. What is a dotenv file?
options: A Docker environment file
A .env file that stores environment variables (like API keys and database URLs) for local development, loaded at runtime
A file that encrypts secrets for production
A global OS environment configuration
questions.explanation: A .env file (dotenv) stores key=value environment variables for local development. Libraries like dotenv automatically load these into process.env. It should never be committed to version control.

questions.q: What does 'docker-compose spins up dependencies' mean in a dev context?
options: Docker Compose deploys to production
Running docker-compose up starts local instances of services the app depends on (database, cache, message broker) without installing them natively
Docker Compose builds the application image
Dependencies are downloaded from Docker Hub directly into the app
questions.explanation: docker-compose.yml defines and starts supporting services locally. A developer runs 'docker-compose up' to get a local Postgres, Redis, or other services running, so the app can connect to them during development.

questions.q: What is a 'seed script' that 'populates the database'?
options: A script that creates the database schema
A script that inserts representative sample data into the database so developers have realistic data to work with locally
A script that backs up the database
A migration script that alters table structure
questions.explanation: A seed script inserts initial or sample data (users, products, test records) into a freshly created database, giving developers a realistic starting state without needing a production data dump.

questions.q: A team mentions 'the README has a getting started in 10 minutes guide'. Why is this important?
options: It replaces the need for documentation
It allows new developers to set up and run the project locally quickly without needing help from teammates
It is required for open-source licensing
It documents the production deployment process
questions.explanation: A concise getting-started guide in the README reduces onboarding friction. A developer who can run the project locally within 10 minutes is productive sooner and less dependent on colleagues for environment setup help.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm getting a 'Connection refused' error when running the tests locally. I've checked my network and it seems fine." Mark (during code review): "Did you try restarting the backend-service ? It might be stuck in a transient state." What does Mark likely mean by suggesting 'restart the backend-service'? Consider the context of running local development tests.
options: It indicates a permanent hardware failure requiring immediate replacement.
It suggests temporarily pausing and resuming the service to clear any temporary issues or resource contention that might be causing the connection error.
The 'Connection refused' error means the client application is intentionally blocking connections from other services.
Restarting the service automatically resolves all network configuration problems, regardless of their root cause.
questions.explanation: Mark is referring to a common troubleshooting step in local development environments - restarting dependent services. A 'Connection refused' error often arises from temporary issues like locked resources or processes not fully shutting down correctly within the service itself. Restarting forces a clean initialization and can resolve these transient problems without requiring a full system reboot, which would be far more disruptive.

questions.q: Liam : "I'm seeing intermittent failures in my local tests - sometimes they pass, sometimes they fail. I've checked the logs and there don't seem to be any obvious errors." David (during code review): "Have you tried restarting the backend-service ? It could be experiencing temporary resource contention." What is David likely referring to when he suggests restarting the backend-service ?
options: A. He needs to upgrade the service's version to a more stable release.
B. The service might be temporarily blocked by a firewall or network issue, and restarting it will resolve this.
C. The service is likely experiencing temporary resource constraints (e.g., memory pressure) that are causing intermittent failures, and a restart will clear these.
D. He should immediately escalate the issue to operations for further investigation, as it's a critical system failure.
questions.explanation: David is using the term 'transient state' which refers to a temporary problem that resolves itself without requiring any permanent changes. Restarting the backend-service is a common troubleshooting step for this kind of issue - it effectively clears out any accumulated resource conflicts or temporarily blocked connections that might be causing the intermittent failures. Option A and D are incorrect because they suggest more serious problems than a transient state, while option B is less precise; restarting simply resets the service's internal state.

The seed script isn't executing properly, meaning it's not populating the database with initial data.

Storing API keys in a .env file prevents them from being accidentally committed to public repositories, safeguarding sensitive credentials.
.env files automatically encrypt all API keys, providing an extra layer of security during local development.
Ben is using .env files to speed up the build process by dynamically loading environment variables.

exercises.title: Makefile & Task Runner Language
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for Makefile targets, prerequisites, task runners, and build automation communication.

questions.q: In a Makefile, a '.PHONY' target declaration is used for:
options: Creating a fake build target for testing purposes.
Declaring that a target name does not correspond to an actual file - telling Make to always run the recipe, even if a file with that name exists in the directory.
Marking a target as deprecated and scheduled for removal.
Creating a target that is shared between multiple build configurations.
questions.explanation: .PHONY prevents Make from treating target names like 'clean', 'build', 'test' as file names. Without .PHONY, if a file named 'clean' existed, 'make clean' would do nothing. .PHONY ensures the recipe always runs.

questions.q: In a Makefile, the phrase 'Run `make install` to install dependencies, then `make build` to compile the project' indicates:
options: A sequential dependency - you must manually run these in order because Make cannot infer the dependency.
Two separate make targets, each with their own recipe. The README documents the manual sequence because the 'build' target has not declared 'install' as its prerequisite.
A Makefile error - targets should be run in parallel, not sequentially.
A build system where 'install' and 'build' share the same recipe but different outputs.
questions.explanation: If build does not list install as a prerequisite, Make won't run install automatically. The README sequence documents the manual workflow. Better practice: make install a prerequisite of build so 'make build' automatically runs 'make install' if needed.

questions.q: Task runner alternatives like 'just' and 'taskfile' are described as being different from Make in that they:
options: Support more programming languages than Make, which only works with C.
Are simpler tools designed purely for running tasks with named commands - without Make's file-dependency-tracking semantics, which can be confusing when used purely as a task runner.
Are only available on Linux and are not cross-platform.
Generate Makefiles automatically from configuration files.
questions.explanation: Make was designed for C compilation dependency management. Using Make purely as a task runner works but can be confusing: .PHONY requirements, tab-only indentation, complex variable expansion. 'just' and 'Taskfile' are purpose-built task runners without the file-dependency complexity.

questions.q: Automatic variables in a Makefile like '$@' and '$<' represent:
options: User-defined variables that are automatically exported to the shell environment.
Built-in variables: $@ is the target name; $
Variables that are automatically imported from environment variables.
Special characters that disable automatic dependency generation.
questions.explanation: Automatic variables enable pattern rules: '%: %.c' with recipe '$(CC) -o $@ $<' compiles any .c file. $@ = current target, $< = first prerequisite (the .c file), $^ = all prerequisites. Without these, you'd need separate rules for every file.

questions.q: The `$(MAKE)` variable should be used instead of `make` inside a Makefile recipe because:
options: It is shorter to type and improves readability.
It ensures the recursive make call uses the same Make executable and flags as the parent invocation - critical for portability and for passing special flags like -j (parallel jobs) down to sub-makes.
It activates special features in Make that are not available with the bare 'make' command.
It prevents infinite recursion when a recipe calls make on the same Makefile.
questions.explanation: Using $(MAKE) for recursive calls ensures flag consistency: if the user runs 'make -j8', sub-makes also run with -j8. Using bare 'make' would lose flags and might use a different Make binary on systems with multiple versions installed.

questions.q: What does 'the workspace package is auto-linked' mean?
options: The package is published to npm automatically
Local workspace packages reference each other without manual install steps - the package manager links them automatically
The package source is downloaded from a CDN
Linking requires running a separate command
questions.explanation: In monorepo workspace setups (npm/yarn/pnpm workspaces), packages within the repo are automatically linked so you can import them as if they were installed from npm.

questions.q: A developer says 'pnpm's strict lockfile prevents phantom dependencies'. What is a phantom dependency?
options: A dependency that is never used
A package that code imports but that is not explicitly declared in package.json - only reachable via hoisting
A dependency with a circular reference
A devDependency accidentally bundled in production
questions.explanation: Phantom dependencies occur when a package is accessible because it was hoisted to node_modules by a parent package, even though it is not declared in your own package.json. pnpm's strict mode prevents this.

questions.q: What does 'the build system only rebuilds affected packages' mean?
options: The build system rebuilds all packages every time
Only packages whose source files changed (or whose dependencies changed) are rebuilt, saving time
The build runs packages in alphabetical order
Only production packages are built
questions.explanation: Modern monorepo build tools like Turborepo and Nx use dependency graphs and caching to skip rebuilding packages that have not changed, drastically reducing build times.

questions.q: What is meant by 'the shared ESLint config is in the root'?
options: Each package has its own independent ESLint config
A single ESLint configuration at the repository root is inherited by all packages, ensuring consistent linting rules
ESLint is only run from the root, not inside packages
The root config disables ESLint for sub-packages
questions.explanation: Monorepos often place shared tooling configs (ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript base) in the root so all packages inherit the same rules, with packages able to extend or override as needed.

questions.q: What does 'workspace protocol (workspace:*)' mean in a monorepo dependency declaration?
options: The package is fetched from a private npm registry
The version range always resolves to the local workspace version of that package, not a published version
The package is only available in development builds
The * means the latest published version

exercises.subtitle: Master npm and yarn vocabulary: package scripts, semantic versioning, package.json fields, and workspace concepts.

questions.q: In package.json, a 'scripts' field entry like 'build: vite build' is run with:
options: node build
npm run build
vite start
npx run build
questions.explanation: Named scripts in the 'scripts' field are run with 'npm run '. The 'start', 'test', and 'build' scripts can also be run with 'npm start', 'npm test', etc.

questions.q: In semantic versioning (semver), a patch version bump (e.g., 1.2.3 to 1.2.4) indicates:
options: A new feature was added.
A backward-incompatible change was made.
A backward-compatible bug fix was made.
The package is being deprecated.
questions.explanation: Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Patch = backward-compatible bug fix. Minor = backward-compatible new feature. Major = breaking change.

questions.q: The caret (^) in a version range like ^2.3.1 in package.json means:
options: Only install exactly version 2.3.1.
Install any version compatible with 2.3.1 (same major: 2.x.x).
Install the latest version available.
Install version 2.3.1 or any higher major version.
questions.explanation: The caret ^ allows minor and patch updates within the same major version - ^2.3.1 allows 2.3.1 up to (but not including) 3.0.0.

questions.q: What is a 'peer dependency' in npm?
options: A dependency shared between two packages in the same project.
A package that the consumer of your library must install separately, because your library needs it but does not bundle it.
A development-only dependency used for testing.
A dependency from a trusted peer organisation.
questions.explanation: Peer dependencies are packages that a library expects the host project to provide - React component libraries list React as a peer dependency rather than bundling their own copy.

questions.q: npm workspaces allow you to:
options: Run multiple npm accounts simultaneously.
Manage multiple packages in a single repository (monorepo) with shared node_modules and cross-package linking.
Create separate npm registries for different teams.
Isolate node_modules for each developer on the team.
questions.explanation: Workspaces enable monorepo development - packages within the workspace can reference each other without publishing, and dependencies are hoisted to a shared node_modules.

questions.q: Sarah : 'Hey team, I'm running into a problem with the build process. It's consistently failing after deploying to staging, and the logs show an error related to a missing dependency. I've checked my package.json and it *looks* correct, but I'm not sure how to properly add a peer dependency for this library.' Which of the following best describes Sarah's situation and what she should consider adding to her project?
options: Adding a `peerDependencies` section to the package.json file, listing all dependencies that this library relies on.
Using the npm install --save-dev command to automatically resolve any missing dependencies based on the current project setup.
Running npm audit fix to automatically update vulnerable packages and potentially identify the root cause of the build failure.
Consulting with a senior developer to review the dependency tree and ensure all required dependencies are correctly listed in the package.json .
questions.explanation: Sarah's situation highlights the importance of explicitly managing peer dependencies. A `peerDependencies` section in package.json clearly specifies which packages this library expects to be installed alongside it-typically other libraries that depend on it. This prevents conflicts and ensures the correct versions are used, avoiding unexpected build failures. Option B is incorrect because automatic dependency resolution isn't always reliable; options C and D represent alternative troubleshooting steps but don't address the core issue of peer dependencies.

questions.q: Liam : 'Hey team, during the code review of PR #123, I noticed you're using a custom build script that calls `node_modules/.bin/some-tool` directly. It's generally better practice to explicitly define aliases in your package.json scripts and then use those aliases instead. This makes the build more reproducible and easier to manage.' Considering Liam's feedback, which of the following actions should Maria take regarding her project's build script?
options: Insufficient - the current approach is working fine and doesn't impact deployment times.
Add a `pre` hook to her package.json that executes the command using npm run some-tool , ensuring the tool is available in the node_modules path.
Define an alias named 'some-tool' within her package.json scripts section and then use ' npm run some-tool ' to execute the build process.
Ignore Liam's suggestion; using node_modules/.bin/ directly is a standard practice and doesn't require any changes.
questions.explanation: Liam's comment highlights a key principle of maintainable projects: reproducibility. Directly calling node_modules/.bin/some-tool relies on the specific environment setup and can break if dependencies change or are updated. Defining an alias in package.json creates a more reliable and consistent build process, making it easier to manage dependencies and ensures that the tool is always available via npm scripts. Option B is the most direct and recommended solution.

questions.q: During a code review of a pull request for a new React component library, David comments: 'I noticed you're directly importing components from the `src/components` directory. While it works now, it's not ideal for maintainability - we should be using npm packages instead. Could you consider publishing this as an npm package?' Maria responds to David with the following message: 'Okay, I understand your point. I've added a npm install command to my project's `package.json` file to manage the component library dependency. It seems to be working fine.' Which of the following statements best reflects Maria's approach and the potential issue she might be facing?
options: Insufficient - Maria is correctly managing dependencies with npm install , and David's suggestion is unnecessary.
Correct - Maria has implemented a standard dependency management practice. The problem lies in David's misunderstanding of the component library's intended use.

Insufficient - Using npm install for a locally developed component doesn't address the core issue of publishing it as an npm package. She should also consider using peer dependencies to manage transitive dependencies.
Insufficient - Maria is correctly managing her project's dependencies, but she hasn't addressed the need for versioning and potentially publishing the library itself as an npm package.
questions.explanation: Maria's approach of simply using npm install to manage a locally developed component is not ideal. While it fulfills the immediate requirement of having the dependency available in her project, it doesn't address the long-term maintainability and potential for reuse that David was highlighting. The core issue is that this component should be treated as an npm package - meaning it needs versioning (using semver), a proper package.json file with scripts for building and testing, and potentially publishing to npm itself. Option 3 correctly identifies this misunderstanding.

However, when I execute npm run deploy , it seems to only run the `build` script once, even though there's also a `deploy:staging` script defined. I'm not sure why this is happening.' Which of the following best explains what might be occurring and how John should troubleshoot this issue?
options: Insufficient - npm scripts always execute sequentially regardless of definitions.

The npm run deploy command executes scripts in alphabetical order, causing `deploy:staging` to be skipped because `build` comes before it alphabetically. John should explicitly use npm run deploy:staging .
npm scripts are executed in the order they appear in package.json . John should reorder his scripts with `deploy:staging` listed before `build` to ensure it runs first.

The problem is likely a misconfiguration within the build script itself, causing it to fail prematurely and prevent the subsequent deployment script from running. John needs to debug the 'build' script.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights an important detail about how npm scripts are executed: they run sequentially in the order specified within the package.json file. When John uses `npm run deploy`, it executes the script named 'deploy' which then runs the `build` script before running any other defined scripts. Therefore, using `npm run deploy:staging` would directly execute the staging deployment script without triggering the build step first; reordering the scripts in package.json wouldn't fix this fundamental behavior.

questions.q: During a code review of PR #456, Ben observes that Alex is using the command `npm install --save-dev eslint` in his project's root directory. He asks Alex: 'I noticed you're installing ESLint as a dev dependency. Do you have any specific configuration or scripts set up to run it during development? Are you intending to use it for linting and formatting, or just as a tool that needs to be available in the project?' Alex responds: 'No, I just wanted to make sure it was installed. I'm not using it yet.' Considering Ben's feedback, what is the MOST appropriate action Alex should take regarding ESLint?
options: Immediately remove `eslint` from package.json and delete the node_modules directory, then run `npm install` again to ensure a clean installation.
Add a configuration file (e.g., .eslintrc.js) and define some basic rules for ESLint, allowing him to start using it during development.
Ignore Ben's comment and continue using ESLint without any configuration; the package manager will automatically handle dependencies.
Contact the project maintainers to ask for guidance on how to properly integrate ESLint into the development workflow.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that Alex should add a configuration file and define some basic rules. Simply installing ESLint as a dev dependency doesn't actually *use* it; he needs to configure it to tell it what to check for. Options A and B are too drastic - removing the dependency without configuring it won't solve anything. Option C is incorrect because npm handles dependencies, but not configuration, and option D suggests unnecessary escalation when a simple solution exists. Configuring ESLint allows Alex to actually leverage its functionality during development.

exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for .npmrc, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml, private registries, and package manager configuration.

questions.q: In an .npmrc file, the 'registry' field controls:
options: The list of npm packages that are allowed to be installed in the project.
Which npm registry server is used to download packages - by default the public npm registry, but organisations often set this to a private registry like Artifactory or GitHub Packages.
The registry of all installed package versions for the current project.
The cache directory where downloaded packages are stored.
questions.explanation: .npmrc registry configuration: registry=https://artifactory.company.com/npm/ redirects all npm installs to the internal registry. Scope-specific overrides: @company:registry=... applies only to @company/* packages, allowing mixed public/private package resolution.

questions.q: The phrase 'we mirror public npm packages to our internal Artifactory registry to ensure build reproducibility' means:
options: The company has copied the npm website to internal servers.

Public packages are cached in the internal registry - builds rely on the internal copy rather than the public npm registry, so builds are not affected by packages being removed from public npm (like the left-pad incident).
Artifactory automatically publishes all internal packages to the public npm registry.
The internal registry only allows packages that have been mirrored, blocking direct internet access.
questions.explanation: The 2016 left-pad incident (package unpublished from npm, breaking thousands of builds worldwide) highlighted the risk of direct dependency on public registries. Internal mirrors/caches provide availability guarantees and security scanning before packages reach developers.

questions.q: In pyproject.toml, the difference between [project.dependencies] and [project.optional-dependencies] is:
options: Required dependencies are installed automatically; optional dependencies are listed for documentation only.

[project.dependencies] lists packages required for the project to run; [project.optional-dependencies] lists packages needed for specific extras (e.g., 'dev' for testing tools, 'docs' for documentation generation) - installed with 'pip install project[dev]'.
Optional dependencies are older dependencies that may be removed in a future version.
Required dependencies are pinned to exact versions; optional dependencies use version ranges.
questions.explanation: Optional dependency groups (extras) allow: pip install mypackage installs only core deps; pip install mypackage[dev] also installs testing/linting tools; pip install mypackage[docs] installs documentation tools. Users only install what they need.

questions.q: In Cargo.toml, the [features] section is used to:
options: Document the features and capabilities of the Rust crate.
Define optional compile-time features that enable/disable code paths or dependencies - users can select features at build time to include only the functionality they need.
List the Rust language features (edition 2021, 2018) the crate uses.
Declare minimum Rust version requirements for specific features.
questions.explanation: Cargo features are compile-time conditional compilation. Example: serde feature = include serde serialisation support. cargo build --features serde enables it; without the flag, that code path is excluded. This reduces binary size and compile time for consumers who don't need every feature.

questions.q: A private package registry vocabulary exercise: 'scoped packages in GitHub Packages require authentication'. This means:
options: GitHub requires payment before packages can be scoped.

Packages published to GitHub Packages under an organisation scope (e.g. @my-org/package) can only be downloaded by authenticated users - developers must configure an access token in .npmrc to install them.
Only packages with an NPM scope can be published to GitHub Packages.
GitHub Packages automatically authenticates using the user's GitHub login without configuration.
questions.explanation: GitHub Packages (unlike public npm) requires a Personal Access Token (PAT) with read:packages scope for downloading. Configuration: //npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .npmrc. CI pipelines pass GITHUB_TOKEN as a secret.

questions.q: What does a developer mean by 'npm run build'?
options: Install all dependencies
Execute the build script defined in package.json
Publish the package to npm
Create a new package.json
questions.explanation: 'npm run build' executes whatever command is defined under the 'build' key in the scripts section of package.json - typically compiling or bundling the project.

questions.q: A colleague says 'the script runs the linter before tests'. What does this imply?
options: Tests run first, then linting
Linting and testing run in parallel
The linter is configured as a prerequisite step before the test script
The linter replaces the test runner
questions.explanation: This describes a script ordering where linting is executed first (often via a 'pretest' hook or explicit chaining) before the test suite runs.

questions.q: What are 'pre/post hooks in package.json scripts'?
options: External CI pipeline steps
Scripts prefixed with 'pre' or 'post' that run automatically before or after a named script
Environment variables loaded before scripts
npm lifecycle events unrelated to custom scripts
questions.explanation: npm automatically runs 'pre ' before and 'post ' after any script named ' '. For example, 'pretest' runs before 'test'.

questions.q: What does 'custom script aliases vocabulary' refer to in a team context?
options: Renaming npm itself
Defining short, memorable script names in package.json that wrap longer commands
Using aliases in the OS shell profile
Aliasing node_modules binaries
questions.explanation: Teams define custom script names like 'dev', 'lint:fix', or 'db:seed' in package.json so developers use consistent, short commands instead of memorizing long CLI strings.

questions.q: A team says 'we standardized all projects on the same script names'. What is the benefit?
options: It reduces the number of dependencies
Developers can run the same commands (build, test, dev) across any project without reading docs first
It prevents merge conflicts in package.json
It removes the need for a CI pipeline
questions.explanation: Standardizing script names (e.g., always 'npm run dev' to start, 'npm run test' to test) means developers can onboard to any project and run familiar commands immediately.

It's a standard practice for deploying to staging environments, providing valuable debugging information without requiring manual intervention.
It's a complex configuration that requires immediate attention from the DevOps team because it bypasses normal deployment procedures.
The script is irrelevant; Liam should be focusing on writing unit tests instead of logging environment details.
questions.explanation: Liam's action-running a script during deployment to log environment details-is a common and beneficial practice. These scripts often contain crucial information for debugging issues in the staging environment before release. The key is that it's *not* an automated test; rather, it provides real-time insights without requiring manual steps. This contrasts with options A, C, and D, which misinterpret the script's purpose or suggest unnecessary complexity.

questions.q: Sarah : 'I'm using a script called `npm start` to run the application locally. It seems straightforward.' During a standup update, you hear Sarah's comment. Which of the following best explains what `npm start` typically does in this context?
options: It automatically deploys the code to production.
It executes the main command defined in the package.json 's "start" script, usually starting a development server.
It validates the code against a set of predefined rules before running it.
It creates a new Git branch for testing changes.
questions.explanation: The `npm start` script is commonly used to execute the command specified in the `"start"` field of the package.json file. This usually involves launching a development server or running other commands needed for local development. It's *not* deployment, validation, or branch creation - those are handled by separate tools and scripts.

questions.q: Mark sends this Slack message: 'Just added a script to package.json that runs before our tests. It's using the eslint command.' What does Mark likely intend to achieve with this pre-test script?
options: Ensure all dependencies are installed before running tests.
Automatically format the code according to team standards.
Run a linter to check for potential errors and style issues in the codebase before executing the tests.
Generate test data based on project requirements.
questions.explanation: Pre-test scripts often utilize linters like eslint to automatically scan code for coding standards violations or potential errors. This helps catch problems early and improve the quality of the codebase before running the actual tests, ensuring a more reliable test execution process. It's distinct from dependency installation or data generation.

questions.q: David is reviewing a pull request and sees this line in the PR description: 'The script includes a post-deploy hook to update the database schema.' What is the primary purpose of a post-deploy hook?
options: It automatically builds the application after deployment.
It runs commands *after* the application has been successfully deployed, typically for tasks like database migrations or configuration updates.
It performs security scans on the deployed application.
It monitors the application's performance during and after deployment.
questions.explanation: Post-deploy hooks are executed *after* an application has been successfully deployed to a server. They're commonly used for tasks such as updating databases, configuring servers, or performing other actions that need to happen once the application is live. This contrasts with pre-deploy hooks which run before deployment.

questions.q: You're discussing 'script aliases' with a colleague. The team has decided to use aliases like `npm run build:prod` instead of `npm run build` . What is the main benefit of using script aliases?
options: It automatically generates documentation for all scripts.
It simplifies complex commands by breaking them down into more readable and maintainable components, improving clarity and reducing errors.
It ensures that all scripts are executed in a specific order.
It allows you to run different versions of the application simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Script aliases provide a shorter, more user-friendly way to invoke complex commands defined within the package.json file. They improve readability and maintainability by abstracting away the underlying command structure, reducing the likelihood of errors when specifying long or complicated scripts. It's about simplifying access.

questions.q: Elena says: 'We're standardizing all our projects on the same set of script names in the package.json - specifically, we're using `npm run build` and `npm run test` across the board.' What is the *most* likely reason for this standardization?
options: To ensure maximum compatibility with all project environments.
To simplify onboarding new developers by providing a consistent command structure.
To enable easier automation of tasks through CI/CD pipelines.
To guarantee that every project always uses the latest version of the build tools.
questions.explanation: Standardizing script names significantly streamlines onboarding for new team members. It provides a predictable and familiar command structure, making it easier for them to understand and use the development tools without needing extensive training on different projects' configurations. Consistency is key in collaborative environments.

exercises.title: Pre-commit Hooks Language
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for pre-commit configuration, hook stages, CI enforcement, and bypass communication.

questions.q: A pre-commit hook is best described as:
options: A script that runs before a pull request is created on GitHub.
A script that runs automatically before each git commit is recorded - allowing automated checks (linting, formatting, tests) to run and potentially block the commit if they fail.
A webhook that notifies a CI system before the code is committed.
A pre-condition check in a CI pipeline before the build starts.
questions.explanation: Pre-commit hooks are local git hooks (.git/hooks/pre-commit) that run checks before the commit is finalised. The pre-commit framework manages these hooks declaratively via .pre-commit-config.yaml - consistent across all developer machines.

questions.q: The phrase 'the pre-commit hook runs `black` and `isort` before each commit to enforce code style' means:
options: Black and isort are run manually before committing as a developer best practice.
Every time a developer runs 'git commit', the hook automatically formats Python code with Black and sorts imports with isort - the commit is blocked if formatting would change any files.
Black and isort are run in CI after the commit is pushed to the remote.
The hook checks that Black and isort are installed on the developer's machine.
questions.explanation: Pre-commit hooks with Black/isort enforce consistent code formatting: they run the formatters and either auto-fix the files (then fail the commit so the developer stages the changes) or block the commit until the developer runs the formatters manually.

questions.q: The command 'git commit --no-verify' is used to:
options: Create an unverified commit that requires additional review before merging.
Bypass all pre-commit hooks - useful in specific situations like committing a partial work-in-progress or when hooks are broken, but should be used sparingly and noted in the commit message.
Verify the commit signature using GPG without running hooks.
Skip only the slow hooks (those taking more than 10 seconds) to save time.
questions.explanation: --no-verify bypasses ALL hooks. It's a last resort: broken hooks blocking urgent work, or deliberately committing incomplete code with a WIP note. Overuse undermines the value of hooks. Teams sometimes audit --no-verify usage in CI by checking commit logs.

questions.q: Running pre-commit checks in CI (in addition to locally) is described as ensuring:
options: Developers always have the pre-commit framework installed on their machines.
Checks cannot be bypassed - even if a developer uses --no-verify locally, the CI pipeline will catch any formatting or lint violations before the code can be merged.
CI runs hooks faster than local machines, improving developer productivity.
Hooks run with production environment variables during CI, matching the deployment context.
questions.explanation: Local hooks + CI hooks is defense-in-depth: local hooks give fast feedback at commit time; CI enforcement catches anything that slipped through (--no-verify, hooks not installed, hooks misconfigured). Without CI, local hooks are purely advisory.

questions.q: In a .pre-commit-config.yaml, the 'stages' key for a hook specifies:
options: The order in which hooks run relative to each other.
Which git events trigger the hook - for example, 'stages: [commit]' runs at git commit; 'stages: [push]' runs at git push; 'stages: [manual]' only runs when explicitly invoked.
The number of parallel processes the hook can use.
Which file types the hook should process.
questions.explanation: Pre-commit supports multiple stages: commit (default), prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, push, post-merge. Expensive checks (unit tests) can be staged to push rather than commit - fast feedback locally, thorough checks before sharing.
